newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - ABARE sees better Australian rate cut chance.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - ABARE sees better Australian rate cut chance.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday the chances of a further Australian monetary policy easing were improving and prime rates were likely to be cut 0.5 percent later this fiscal year.

"The prospect for further reductions in Australian interest rates in the short term has improved, given the outlook for continued low inflation and the fiscal tightening announced in the 1996/97 (July-June) budget," the bureau said in its quarterly Australian Commodities publication.
"ABARE has assumed that prime lending rates will be reduced by around 0.5 percent later in 1996/97, to average around 10.2 percent for the year, compared with an average of 10.8 percent in 1995/96."
The Australian dollar was assumed to average US$0.7700 and 57 points on the Reserve Bank's trade-weighted index in 1996/97, compared with US$0.7600 and 55 points in 1995/96.
The currency was trading at US$0.7900 early on Tuesday and at 58.2 on the trade-weighted index.
The bureau's forecast faster inflation than Treasury did in the August budget.
"ABARE has assumed that Australia's headline inflation rate will decline to an annual average of 2.3 percent in 1996/97 from 4.2 percent in 1995/96," it said.
The Treasury forecasts 2.0 percent year-average inflation -- average prices in 1996/97 compared with the average for 1995/96.
Under the bureau's own definition of core inflation -- excluding the effects of interest rate changes -- annual price rises would average 3.0 percent in 1996/97, down from 3.6 percent previously.

"Other price indices released recently (apart from the consumer price index) also indicate that inflationary pressures are likely to remain low in the short term," the bureau said, noting falling import prices as an example.

"Pressures on wage growth in Australia also moderated with average weekly earnings increasing by 3.9 percent in the year ended May 1996, compared with 4.2 percent in the year ended February 1996 and 4.9 percent in the year ended November 1995."
The bureau's GDP forecast was a touch weaker than Treasury's: 3.3 percent year-average for 1996/97, compared with the 3.5 percent shown in the budget papers.
Actual GDP growth in 1995/96 was 4.1 percent.
The Reserve Bank of Australia eased monetary policy on July 31, dropping its overnight cash rate target to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent, where it had remained since December 1994.
